t: Introduction: norms of morality and law
n: Introduction to the topic: norms of morality and law. In society relations are governed by social norms that embody norms of morality and law. Norms of morality consist of ethics, the requirements of religion and customs; their observance is secured by the force of public opinion. Norms of law are introduced by the state, apply equally to everyone and are secured by state compulsion. That is, the main difference is in how observance of the norm is secured.

Professional offences of medical workers, abbreviated POMW. The activity of medical workers is determined by law and other normative documents. Failure to meet, or improper meeting of, the requirements established in medical activity is called POMW. Remember: this concept covers both complete failure to meet a requirement and its improper performance.

t: Difference between a misdemeanour and a crime
n: The difference between a misdemeanour and a crime. If an unlawful act has no feature of social danger and is not provided for by the Criminal Code, it is called a misdemeanour. Where there are features of social danger, the same act is assessed as a crime. A misdemeanour has no feature of social danger and is not provided for by the Criminal Code. A crime has features of social danger; it is a guilty socially dangerous act prohibited under threat of punishment.

t: Types of misdemeanour of medical workers
n: Types of misdemeanour of medical workers. From the standpoint of law, misdemeanours of medical workers are divided into disciplinary, administrative and civil. In a disciplinary misdemeanour the established order of work, service and production is violated. In an administrative offence the order of managing the institution is violated. A civil misdemeanour means violation of the property and non-property rights of citizens and organisations.

The term "medical error" and Pirogov. The expression "medical error" was first proposed by N. I. Pirogov. Pirogov stressed that a doctor has the right to err, but no right to conceal errors. He wrote that he had made it a rule never to conceal his errors and failures. This thought remains to this day the chief model of attitude towards medical error.

Davydovsky's definition. Davydovsky in 1928 defined medical error thus: it is a conscientious mistake resulting from imperfection of medical science and methods, atypical course of the disease, or insufficient preparation of the doctor. There must be no elements of negligence, inattention or medical ignorance. That is, the definition names three causes and requires absence of elements of negligence as a condition of a conscientious mistake.

Medical error and legal liability. "Medical error" must not mean cases in which, from the legal point of view, there is a crime or an administrative, disciplinary or civil misdemeanour. The adverse consequences of a "conscientious mistake" should, by logic, not give rise to legal liability. They should be disclosed and discussed among colleagues so as not to be repeated.

t: Case analysis: presentation with abdominal pain
n: Case analysis: presentation with abdominal pain. A man aged 30 presented with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting and one loose stool; BP 110/70, pulse 90. The doctor, suspecting food poisoning, decided to wash out the stomach. When the tube was passed the patient suddenly died. At autopsy acute myocardial infarction, the abdominal form, was found. Sequence of events: abdominal pain and vomiting, suspicion of poisoning, passing of the tube, sudden death, myocardial infarction at autopsy.

Historical example: Krassovsky, 1870. Krassovsky removed an ovarian cyst; the woman died 40 hours later. At pathological anatomical examination a sponge tampon left in the abdominal cavity was found. Krassovsky considered it his duty to describe this in an article and set out the case openly. He proposed counting sponges in surgery and attaching a long tape. Here is seen a model of not concealing an error and drawing conclusions from it against repetition.

The concept of accident. An accident is an adverse outcome caused by circumstances not dependent on medical workers, which could not be foreseen or removed. In most cases such outcomes arise from individual features of organs not identified during life. That is, the doctor could not know of this danger beforehand and could not remove it.

The term "iatrogenesis". "Iatrogenesis" derives from the Greek words iatros, that is, doctor, and gennao, that is, I give rise to. It was proposed in 1925 by the German psychiatrist O. Bumke. At first it meant illnesses caused by the adverse effect of the doctor's words or actions on the patient's psyche. Kassirsky proposed including in the concept also incorrect performance of procedures and incorrect use of drugs.

t: Current interpretation of iatrogenesis and types
n: Current interpretation of iatrogenesis and types. According to the current generally accepted interpretation, iatrogenesis is a new pathological state arising under the action of medical factors. The medical factor includes all elements of medical technology and the conditions of the institution where the patient is. Types: diagnostic, therapeutic, that is, surgical and physical, psycho-emotional and informational, preventive, non-treatment, that is, late presentation, and others.

Crime: general features. Features of a crime: danger to society, criminal unlawfulness, guilt and provision for punishment. A guilty socially dangerous act prohibited under threat of punishment is recognised as a crime; this is stated in Article 14 of the Criminal Code. Only an act that the law classifies as a crime is a criminally punishable offence. These four features together define a crime.

Guilt: intent and negligence. Guilt is understood as commission of a socially dangerous act under the control of human consciousness and will. A person is found guilty of intent or negligence, as given in Article 20 of the Criminal Code. In direct intent the person realised the danger, foresaw the consequences and desired them; this is Article 21. In indirect intent he foresaw the consequences and consciously allowed them to occur. Negligence is divided into the forms of overconfidence and carelessness.

Negligence: overconfidence and carelessness. In overconfidence the person, seeing the possibility of consequences, without observing precautions, groundlessly hopes they will not occur. In carelessness the person did not foresee the consequences, but should and could have foreseen them; this is Article 22. In most cases medical workers are held liable for crimes committed through negligence.

Case analysis: examples of negligence. First example: the duty surgeon and anaesthetist, without reason, without preparation, without an assistant and nurse, performed an elective abdominal operation, and a serious outcome occurred. This is overconfidence. Second example: the doctor did not follow the current standards, and a complication caused the patient's death. The doctor was obliged to know the standards, so this is carelessness. In both examples the type of outcome is distinguished by the form of negligence.

Circumstances excluding a crime. Circumstances that exclude an act's being a crime: justified risk connected with the profession, and extreme necessity. In extreme necessity, if the danger cannot be averted by other measures and the harm caused is less than the harm prevented, the act is not a crime; this is in Article 38. The logic is: danger exists, there is no other measure, the harm is less, so it is not a crime.

Justified risk, Article 41 of the Criminal Code. Risk is regarded as justified if the action is consistent with modern scientific and technical knowledge, the aim could not be achieved without risk, and measures were taken to prevent harm. In justified risk, even if the result is not achieved, no liability for the harm caused arises. Exception: risk taken with knowledge of the danger of loss of life or grave consequences is not regarded as justified.

Case analysis: cardiac wound. A patient with a stab-incised wound of the chest was brought to a district hospital; injury of the heart was established. The conditions for a heart operation do not exist, the patient cannot be transferred, and before the specialist arrives the patient may die. The duty surgeon decided to suture the cardiac wound. This decision is assessed as the only correct one and as justified risk.

The subject of criminal liability. Criminal liability is established for sane natural persons; in most cases for persons who have reached 16 years at the time of the crime, this being Article 17. Sanity is the ability to realise the socially dangerous nature of one's act and to control one's actions. Insanity is determined by two criteria. Medical criterion: mental illness, temporary disorder of the psyche, mental deficiency. Legal criterion: failure to realise the significance of the actions or inability to control them.

Elements of the corpus delicti. The features of a criminal act established by law are called the corpus delicti, and it consists of four elements. The object is that to which harm was done: in crimes of medical workers usually the health and life of citizens. The objective side includes the external manifestation, the consequence, the causal connection between the act and the consequence, and also place, time, method and means.

t: Corpus delicti: subject and subjective side
n: Corpus delicti: subject and subjective side. The subject is the natural person who committed the act: more often doctors, sometimes mid-level and junior staff; managers are subjects of crimes against the order of administration. The subjective side is the person's mental attitude to the act: guilt, motive and purpose. The motive is the impulse and desire that prompted the striving towards the crime, and the purpose is the result one wants to achieve. Thus the corpus consists of the object, objective side, subject and subjective side.

t: Groups of crimes of medical workers
n: Groups of crimes of medical workers. Crimes against health and life: homicide through negligence, Article 102 of the Criminal Code; bodily injuries, 104, 105, 109, 111; failure to perform professional duties, 116; leaving in danger, 117. Criminal abortion, Article 114, and also spread of venereal disease or AIDS, Article 113, belong to this group too. Crimes against the order of administration: negligence in office, 207; forgery in office, 209; taking a bribe, 210; giving a bribe, 211.

t: Improper performance of professional duties (Article 116 of the Criminal Code)
n: Improper performance of professional duties, Article 116 of the Criminal Code. Failure to perform or improper performance of professional duties through negligence or dishonesty, causing harm to health of moderate severity or grave, entails criminal liability. Under the second part, if a person obliged to give help did not give it without a valid reason and harm was caused, a stricter penalty is set. If it caused death of people or other grave consequences, a still stricter penalty is set. So penalty levels rise with the gravity of the consequence.

Obligation to give emergency aid. Article 30 of the Law on the Protection of Citizens' Health: medical and pharmaceutical workers are obliged to give emergency medical aid. If necessary, aid is given regardless of place and time, that is, outside a medical institution and outside working hours. Pre-medical primary aid at the scene must be given by police, fire safety and transport workers.

Valid and invalid reasons. Valid, that is, objective reasons: the worker's own illness, being occupied with aid to a more seriously ill patient, absence of drugs, instruments and transport, natural disasters. Not valid reasons: days off and holidays, non-working time, leave, lack of knowledge for emergency aid, hostility towards the patient. Remember: the question whether reasons are valid is decided by the court.

Three conditions of liability, according to Vermel. First condition: the actions are objectively wrong and contrary to the current instructions, rules and standards. Second condition: the worker, in accordance with his training and category, realises that the action is wrong and has a real possibility of making the right decision. Third condition: the action or omission has a direct causal connection with a serious adverse outcome. The same conditions are needed for civil liability.

Criminal abortion, Article 114: general provisions. Article 114, part 1: artificial termination of pregnancy by an obstetrician-gynaecologist outside medical institutions or where it is medically impossible. Part 2 relates to carrying this out by a person who has no right to terminate pregnancy artificially. The object is the health and life of the pregnant woman; the subjective side is intent; the motive is most often personal gain.

Conditions permitting termination of pregnancy. At the woman's wish, pregnancy can be terminated in specialised institutions up to 12 weeks. With social indications up to 22 weeks, and with medical indications termination is permitted regardless of the term. The list of social indications is determined by the Cabinet of Ministers, that of medical indications by the Ministry of Health.

t: Medical contraindications to termination of pregnancy
n: Medical contraindications to termination of pregnancy. Medical contraindications: pregnancy of more than 12 weeks; acute infectious diseases. Also acute and subacute inflammatory diseases of the genital organs, and also purulent foci regardless of location. The last contraindication: less than 6 months have passed since the last abortion.

Abortion: circumstances determining liability. When carried out outside an institution, the presence or absence of medical contraindications is not taken into account; the term and method are also immaterial. If grave bodily harm is caused, Article 104 applies, that is, intentional infliction of grave bodily harm; in death or other grave consequences, part 3 of Article 114. When the woman herself terminated the pregnancy and in a state of extreme necessity, no criminal liability arises.

Venereal diseases and HIV, Article 113. The subject is usually a person with a venereal disease or HIV; knowing of his illness, he may infect another or put him at risk. In 2010 the liability of medical workers was introduced into the article: if infection with HIV/AIDS resulted from improper performance of professional duties, this is item 5; the object is the patient. The purpose of the change is to prevent the spread of HIV/AIDS.

Offences in office: the subject. Offences in office are against the order of administration; those more often seen in medicine are: abuse, 205; exceeding authority, 206; negligence in office, 207; forgery, 209; bribe, 210. The subject is only an official, that is, a person with administrative-economic, organisational, dispositive and supervisory powers. Among medical workers these are heads of institutions and their deputies, heads of departments, laboratories and pharmacies, chief or senior nurses.

t: When a doctor becomes an official
n: When does a doctor become an official? Doctors and mid-level medical workers are not regarded as officials during diagnosis, treatment and prevention. In certain cases they are recognised as officials: issuing a certificate of incapacity for work, determining disability, attestation, awarding a category, fitness for military service. Three features of an offence in office: violation of a duty, features of social danger, a causal connection between the offence and the consequence.

t: Abuse of authority and exceeding authority
n: Abuse of authority and exceeding authority. Abuse: as a result of deliberate use of official powers, harm or damage is caused in a large amount; for example, refusing to admit a patient. Exceeding authority: deliberately performing an act not provided for. For example, the chief doctor deciding alone a matter to be decided jointly, or issuing a certificate for 30 days. The difference is that in the first the powers are used deliberately, and in the second an act not provided for by the powers is performed.

Negligence in office. If an official's failure to perform his duties through indifference caused damage in a large amount, bodily injury or death, this is negligence in office. Examples: gross violation of the sanitary-epidemiological order and spread of hospital-acquired infection; violation of safety technique in physiotherapy and electrical injury. Responsible managers may be held criminally liable; this crime is committed mainly through negligence.

t: Forgery in office and taking a bribe
n: Forgery in office and taking a bribe. Forgery in office: out of mercenary interest knowingly entering false information into an official document or falsifying it; for example, not recording a rib fracture. Taking a bribe: using official position knowingly to receive material valuables or property benefit for performing or not performing an act. Extortionate demand for payment, Article 214, is not an offence in office; its subject may be practically any medical worker.

Crimes against justice. Of medical workers, forensic medical and forensic psychiatric experts more often become subjects of these crimes. False testimony: an expert knowingly giving a wrong conclusion, Article 238 of the Criminal Code; likewise compelling false testimony by bribe or pressure. Unauthorised disclosure of the secrets of the investigation, 239, and evasion of giving testimony or a conclusion, 240, are regarded as crimes.

t: The expert and failure to report a crime
n: The expert and failure to report a crime. Article 16 of the Law on Forensic Examination and Article 68 of the Code of Criminal Procedure set out the expert's duties. The head of the state forensic expert institution must warn the expert of criminal liability, obtain a receipt and send it with the conclusion; this is Article 14. Article 241 of the Criminal Code: knowing failure to report a grave or especially grave crime. It is advisable that staff report to law enforcement bodies and record it in a document.

Let us summarise. A professional offence is a misdemeanour or a crime; a misdemeanour is disciplinary, administrative or civil. Medical error, that is, a conscientious mistake, and accident do not entail legal liability, but must be analysed. Criminal liability arises only when there are guilt, a corpus delicti and a causal connection.
